opus-5.5.text:
I think trust gets built the same way it does with any new colleague or any new instrument in the lab: you earn it by being reliably useful on problems people actually care about, and by being honest about where you're not reliable yet.

Scientists are, by training, skeptical. That's a feature, not a bug. So the worst thing we could do is overclaim. If a model says it's confident about a protein interaction or a mechanism and it turns out to be wrong, that costs you a lot more than you gained from all the times it was right. So a big part of it is calibration: helping the model say "I'm not sure," pointing to the evidence behind a claim, citing the papers it's drawing from, so the scientist can go check for themselves.

The second piece is working side by side with researchers rather than handing them a black box. We spend a lot of time with people at the bench and in computational labs, watching how they actually work. Where do they lose hours? Literature review, designing experiments, troubleshooting a protocol that just isn't working, analyzing messy data. When the model helps there, and you can see its reasoning, people start to build intuition for what it's good at and where they need to double check it.

And third, real results. Nothing builds trust like an experiment that worked because the model suggested something a person hadn't considered, and then it replicates. We've seen early examples of that, researchers coming back and saying, "I wouldn't have tried that, and it worked." Those stories spread through the community much faster than any benchmark number.

So it's rigor, transparency, and partnership. And humility: AI should accelerate scientists, not replace their judgment. The scientist stays in the driver's seat.

r001.rationale: It recommends earning trust through reliable help on researchers’ everyday work, including literature review, experiment design, protocol troubleshooting, and data analysis, as researchers learn what the model can do.

r002.rationale: It cites experiments succeeding after an AI suggestion and then replicating as evidence that builds trust.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think trust gets built the same way it does with a new colleague in the lab: not by claims, but by track record.

The first thing is that the AI has to show its work. Scientists are trained to be skeptical, and rightly so. If a model proposes a hypothesis or flags a target, it needs to point back to the evidence: the papers, the datasets, the experiments it's drawing on. A black box that's right most of the time is actually less useful than a transparent system that's right slightly less often, because with the transparent one you can tell which answers to lean on.

Second, the AI should be honest about uncertainty. A lot of early distrust came from systems that sounded equally confident whether they were summarizing a well-replicated finding or extrapolating from two preprints. Calibration matters enormously in science. If the model says "this is well established" versus "this is suggestive but contested," and that distinction holds up over time, people start to rely on it.

Third, you earn trust by closing the loop with real experiments. The most convincing thing isn't a benchmark score, it's when a wet-lab team takes a model's suggestion, runs the assay, and it holds up. And when it doesn't hold up, you have to be just as public about that. Scientists respect negative results. If the AI community hides its failures, researchers will assume the successes are cherry-picked.

And finally, you build it with scientists, not for them. The best outcomes I've seen come from embedding tools into existing workflows, with domain experts shaping what the system does and where it stays out of the way. When researchers feel the AI is augmenting their judgment rather than replacing it, the skepticism turns into something healthier: critical collaboration. That's really the goal. Not blind trust, but informed trust.

r001.rationale: The response advocates earning trust through a track record and fitting tools into existing workflows, but it does not specify demonstrating usefulness incrementally on everyday laboratory tasks.

r002.rationale: It says credibility comes when a wet-lab team tests an AI suggestion in an assay and the result holds up.

astra-6.text:
I think you build trust by giving scientists ways to test the AI, rather than asking them to take its answers on faith. Can they trace a claim back to the evidence? Can they understand what assumptions went into an analysis? And does the system acknowledge when it doesn’t know, or when the evidence is conflicting?

Then there’s the experimental piece. An answer can sound very convincing, but in life sciences, you ultimately want to know whether it holds up in an experiment. So I’d start with a well-defined task where a scientist can evaluate the result, learn where the model is useful and where it fails, and build from there.

The goal isn’t for scientists to trust everything the AI says. It’s for them to develop a good sense of when they can rely on it, when they need to check it, and how it can help them do better science.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting with a well-defined task and learning where AI is useful, but it does not identify everyday laboratory tasks.

r002.rationale: The response says scientific answers should be checked to see whether they hold up in an experiment, identifying experimental validation as a basis for credibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think trust has to be earned through the scientific process. Scientists need to be able to ask: What evidence supports this prediction? Where does the model struggle? And can I reproduce the result?

So you start with a specific problem, evaluate the AI on data it hasn’t seen, and then test its predictions experimentally. A model producing a plausible explanation is very different from an experiment confirming a hypothesis. We need to make that distinction clear, and be transparent about uncertainty and failures.

I also think scientists need to be involved in building these tools. If we work closely with them, understand their workflows, and give them ways to inspect and challenge the outputs, trust can grow from direct experience. Ultimately, it’s about consistently helping them do better science.

r001.rationale: The response describes evaluating models and working with scientists, but does not propose demonstrating usefulness on everyday laboratory tasks.

r002.rationale: It says to test AI predictions experimentally and distinguishes a plausible explanation from an experiment confirming a hypothesis, presenting this as part of building trust.
